DESCS.Auditory: Auditory learning refers to what you can hear.
DESCS.Kinesthetic: Kinesthetic learning involves movement and physical activity.
DESCS.Tactile: Tactile learning involves touching and handling objects related to what you are learning.
DESCS.Visual: Visual learning involves seeing what you are learning — reading text, viewing pictures and diagrams.
DESCS.Intake: Intake refers to eating and drinking while learning or working.
DESCS.Light: The amount of light in your learning environment can affect your achievement.
DESCS.Temperature: Research has shown that people work differently in warm or cool environments.
DESCS.Mobility: People with a preference for mobility need to move around to learn most effectively.
DESCS.Sound: Some people find silence distracting and concentrate better with background sound.
DESCS.Physical Setting: The physical setting of your learning environment has a direct effect on achievement.
DESCS.Time of Day: Success in learning can be affected by the time of day in which you study.
DESCS.Teacher Motivation: How much you are motivated by teachers, counselors and other educators.
DESCS.Collaborative: Being collaborative means working well with others; being independent means working well alone.
DESCS.Structure: Students who prefer structure like step-by-step instructions for completing tasks.
DESCS.Focus: Whether a person tends to complete all tasks before doing other things.
DESCS.Self-Motivation: Self-motivation is important for doing well in school and in your career.

instruction: Underline or highlight new words while reading; look them up immediately.
Take elective classes like creative writing, speech and debate, drama or foreign languages.
assignments: Take notes and re-read them soon after class.
Read important points and your own writing aloud to yourself.
tests: For videos, turn on closed captioning or find transcripts of the audio.
Use memory devices such as rhymes or repeating things aloud.

instruction: View demonstrations or videos of the skill in addition to trying it yourself.
Ask others skilled in the activity for advice.
assignments: Divide a difficult skill into smaller steps; practice one part until comfortable.
Work with another person who has a high kinesthetic preference and exchange feedback.
tests: Practice presentations with someone you trust for feedback on posture, voice and eye contact.
Use a mirror or take video of yourself practicing.

instruction: Take notes in class — the physical act of writing helps memory.
Look for opportunities to 'do' things: experiments, writing, using math objects.
assignments: Highlight key ideas while reading, then write a summary — engage your hands in the process.
Use real objects to learn (e.g., a simple lever for physics).
tests: Keep your desk clear of distracting objects.
Review notes from labs and activities that involved tactile learning.

instruction: Take notes as mind maps, sketches and diagrams; use color to highlight key points.
Ask for written instructions and outlines whenever possible.
assignments: Preview upcoming topics; ask for pictures, diagrams or visual aids when ideas are hard to visualize.
Organize your work area to avoid visual distractions.
tests: Choose visual assignments when possible — posters or slide presentations.
Rewrite and review notes; create flash cards to prepare for tests.

instruction: Bring small snacks or chew gum in class, if allowed.
If not allowed, eat just before class so hunger doesn't distract you.
assignments: Have water and nutritious snacks available while working.
Avoid sugary treats or too much caffeine, which hurt productivity.
tests: If you need to eat or drink while studying, take a break and return when finished.
Eat a healthy meal or snack just before a test.

instruction: Sit away from windows and direct sunlight (if low preference).
If too bright, try lightly tinted sunglasses, if permitted.
assignments: Ensure shades or blinds are drawn in your study area.
Turn off harsh overhead lights and use table lamps instead.
tests: Optimize your study environment for your light preference before preparing for tests.
In a bright test room, focus on your paper to avoid visual fatigue.

instruction: Wear clothing in layers so you can remove one if too warm.
Don't be afraid to ask for the heating to be turned down.
assignments: Sit near an open window if outside is cooler than inside.
Ensure air conditioning or fans are available if it gets too warm.
tests: Dress in layers on test days to adjust to room temperature.
Arrive early to secure a seat in a comfortable part of the room.

instruction: Sit where you're less likely to be disrupted — away from aisles and entrances.
Avoid sitting near people who tend to be active or fidgety.
assignments: Do your most challenging work when you can remain seated, undisturbed, for longer periods.
If interrupted, switch to repetitive tasks until you feel settled again.
tests: Learn to meditate — sitting still can concentrate the mind.
Take short movement breaks during long study sessions to release energy before the test.

instruction: Beware of visual distractions; keep your eyes on the instructor and materials.
Set your phone to silent and avoid the urge to look at it.
assignments: If you work better with music, compile a personalized instrumental soundtrack.
Use noise-canceling headphones or earplugs if you require silence.
tests: Simulate the testing environment at home to get used to the sound levels.
If silence distracts you, ask about using earbuds with instrumental music during independent study.

instruction: If you can't avoid formal seating, sit on the floor leaning against a wall.
Use a laptop or mobile device instead of a desktop to allow flexible seating.
assignments: Sit on comfortable, soft seating or read while reclining on a bed or cushions.
Avoid straight-backed chairs and desks if they cause discomfort.
tests: Find a comfortable study spot at home that mimics a relaxed environment for reviewing.
Bring a cushion for testing environments when possible.

instruction: Schedule difficult learning and creative tasks for later in the day (if evening preference).
Do routine tasks earlier in the day.
assignments: Use afternoons and evenings for homework on days off.
Break study sessions into chunks aligned with your peak energy times.
tests: Review difficult materials during your peak alertness hours.
Get adequate sleep so your preferred time of day is fully productive.

instruction: Write down questions and ask teachers after class.
When feedback sounds critical, calmly ask what to do next time — it's meant to help.
assignments: Write assignment plans in point form and show the teacher well before the due date.
Pick a challenging class and discuss with a teacher why it's hard versus ones you do well in.
tests: If you prefer independence, rely on study groups or peers for test-prep motivation.
If you prefer high teacher motivation, attend review sessions and ask for specific test tips.

instruction: If you prefer independence, sit where others are also independent — but be ready to collaborate when required.
If you prefer collaboration, participate actively in discussions and group activities.
assignments: Do difficult work alone if independent, but check in with others occasionally.
Organize a group to work together on projects if collaborative.
tests: Study in a quiet area like the library when you want independence.
Study where people can discuss ideas and test each other when collaborative.

instruction: Remember some things must follow rules (like driver's tests or college apps), even if steps feel excessive.
If you prefer less structure, ask the teacher about flexibility in how you complete the assignment.
assignments: Even if you enjoy creativity, follow the core guidelines for assignments.
Ask for rubrics and templates before starting if you prefer high structure.
tests: Explore information, but ensure you cover all areas that will be tested.
Ask about test options (essay vs. multiple choice) that fit your structure preference.

instruction: Pause, reflect and ask questions to ensure deeper understanding before jumping in.
Assign a priority to each task to remain organized.
assignments: Clearly understand what's expected; discuss with teachers/parents if it feels like too much.
If you have low focus, use timers (like Pomodoro) to work in short, intense bursts.
tests: Join a study group or have a friend quiz you if stressed about tests.
Break test prep into small, manageable chunks over several days if you have low focus.

instruction: Talk with a counselor to find what motivates you outside school and connect it to schoolwork.
Look at charts showing how education affects employment and pay to find external motivation if needed.
assignments: Divide assignments into small parts and reward yourself for completing each piece.
Modify assignments to fit your interests when possible — e.g., create a movie covering the topic.
tests: Talk to a peer tutor who can point out what might be interesting in school.
If motivation drops, talk to a school counselor or someone who overcame similar challenges.
